title: Article 5: liberty and security
subtitle: The six grounds for detention, procedural safeguards, and the corrected deprivation-of-liberty test after the 2026 overruling of the Cheshire West acid test
objectives: State the six permitted grounds of detention under Article 5(1)(a)-(f) and identify which, if any, applies on a given fact pattern
Explain the procedural safeguards in Article 5(2)-(5) and the function each performs in preventing arbitrary detention
State the current test for identifying a deprivation of liberty and explain precisely how and why it differs from the Cheshire West 'acid test' it replaced
Apply the current deprivation-of-liberty test to care, supported-living and family-care fact patterns without defaulting to the superseded acid-test formulation

leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that the line between deprivation of and mere restriction upon liberty is one of degree and intensity, assessed on the concrete situation, not of nature or substance — this general principle survives the 2026 overruling intact

leadingAuthorities.citation: P v Cheshire West and Chester Council [2014] UKSC 19 (overruled in part)
leadingAuthorities.role: Formulated the 'acid test' — continuous supervision and control, and not free to leave — as the sole determinant of a deprivation of liberty; this specific formulation was overruled in part in 2026

leadingAuthorities.citation: A Reference by the Attorney General for Northern Ireland [2026] UKSC 16
leadingAuthorities.role: Handed down 2 June 2026: overrules the Cheshire West acid test and restates the current test for identifying a deprivation of liberty — the central authority for this lesson

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is one of the few lessons in the catalogue where the settled textbook answer changed within the last few months. Where the profile shows a student learned this topic before June 2026, this note appears: 'What you learned about Cheshire West's acid test used to be the whole answer. As of 2 June 2026, it isn't — read this lesson as a correction, not a refresher.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the six grounds and the safeguards well. The test pool below leans hard on applying the corrected post-2026 deprivation-of-liberty test to new facts — that's the skill this lesson is really testing.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and build the six grounds and the safeguards solidly first — Parts 4 and 5, on what changed in 2026, assume you already have that structure in place.

overview.hook: For twelve years, one sentence decided whether tens of thousands of people in care homes, supported living and even their own family homes were, in law, detained: continuous supervision and control, and not free to leave. On 2 June 2026, the Supreme Court decided that sentence was no longer the law. This lesson is not a historical survey of Article 5 doctrine — it teaches the law exactly as it now stands, and it spends real time on what changed, why, and what the old test got wrong, because in this lesson, citing the old textbook answer is not a partial credit answer. It is a wrong one.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. This lesson's central point is a live and very recent development: on 2 June 2026, the Supreme Court in A Reference by the Attorney General for Northern Ireland [2026] UKSC 16 overruled the 'acid test' for identifying a deprivation of liberty set out in P v Cheshire West and Chester Council [2014] UKSC 19. Do not answer on the basis of the Cheshire West acid test as though it remains the current law on that point — it does not. Part 4 of this lesson explains what the acid test said and why it was overruled; Part 5 teaches the corrected test that now applies. Every test-pool item on deprivation of liberty is written against the corrected, post-2026 position.

parts.heading: Article 5's structure: liberty is the default, detention the exception
parts.voice: doctrine-in-motion — opens by flagging that one part of this map was redrawn in 2026, before building the parts that didn't move
body: Article 5 protects the right to liberty and security of person. Its structure inverts the usual Convention pattern: rather than stating a right and then listing permitted limitations in the same paragraph, Article 5(1) states the right and then provides an exhaustive list of six grounds — (a) to (f) — on which a person may lawfully be deprived of their liberty. If detention does not fit one of the six, it is unlawful under Article 5, regardless of how sensible or well-intentioned it was.

Two structural features carry through everything in this lesson. First, 'exhaustive' is doing real work: states cannot invent a seventh ground by domestic statute. Second, any detention within one of the six grounds must also be 'lawful' and 'in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law' — a domestic legal basis is necessary but not sufficient; the detention must also fit one of the six purposes.

Most of this lesson's grounds and safeguards are stable, well-settled doctrine. One question underneath all of them — what actually counts as a 'deprivation of liberty' in the first place, as opposed to a lesser restriction — was substantially rewritten in June 2026. Parts 2 and 3 build the settled structure; Parts 4 and 5 deal with what changed and why it matters.

components.definition: The threshold concept that triggers Article 5 protection at all. A restriction on movement that does not amount to a deprivation of liberty falls outside Article 5 entirely, however inconvenient it is for the person affected — which is exactly why how this line is drawn matters so much, and why the 2026 change is this lesson's centrepiece.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you Article 5(1) cannot be satisfied on these facts.
interaction.scenarioText: A local authority holds a person in a secure unit, relying on a ground it describes as 'detention in the public interest, where the authority judges it appropriate' — a ground that does not correspond to any of Article 5(1)(a) to (f).
tappableSpans: local authority holds a person in a secure unit
does not correspond to any of Article 5(1)(a) to (f)
interaction.correctSpan: does not correspond to any of Article 5(1)(a) to (f)
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Article 5(1)'s list is exhaustive. A domestically invented ground, however reasonable it sounds, cannot itself satisfy Article 5 — the detention must fit one of the six recognised grounds.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The other facts describe how the detention operates in practice; the decisive legal problem is that the stated ground isn't one of the six Article 5(1) grounds at all.

parts.heading: The six gates: Article 5(1)(a)-(f)
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Learn these as a checklist you actively test facts against, not a list to recognise passively. Problem questions will rarely announce which ground is in play; you are expected to identify it, or to notice that none applies.

Two of the six deserve particular care in application questions. Ground (c) — arrest or detention on reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence, or to prevent an offence or fleeing after having done so — is the ordinary criminal-process ground, and it is tightly tied to the purpose of bringing the person before a court. Ground (e) — the 'unsound mind' ground, alongside alcoholics, drug addicts, vagrants and the prevention of spreading infectious disease — is the one most often in play in the care and deprivation-of-liberty fact patterns this lesson builds toward.

components.label: Article 5(1): the six permitted grounds for detention
points: (a) Lawful detention after conviction by a competent court
(b) Lawful detention for non-compliance with a court order, or to secure fulfilment of an obligation prescribed by law
(c) Lawful arrest or detention on reasonable suspicion of an offence, or reasonably necessary to prevent an offence or fleeing after committing one
(d) Detention of a minor for the purpose of educational supervision, or lawful detention to bring a minor before the competent legal authority
(e) Lawful detention of persons of unsound mind, alcoholics, drug addicts or vagrants, or for the prevention of the spreading of infectious diseases
(f) Lawful arrest or detention to prevent unauthorised entry, or of a person against whom action is being taken with a view to deportation or extradition

interaction.prompt: A person with a diagnosed mental disorder is detained in a hospital for assessment and treatment, under a domestic mental health statute. Which Article 5(1) ground most directly applies?
options: Ground (e) — lawful detention of persons of unsound mind
Ground (c) — arrest on reasonable suspicion of an offence
Ground (a) — detention after conviction
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is the classic ground (e) fact pattern, and the one most closely connected to the deprivation-of-liberty case law later in this lesson.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: No offence or conviction is involved here — the detention is for treatment, which is squarely ground (e).

parts.heading: Procedural safeguards: information, review, compensation
parts.voice: systematic — treats the safeguards as a single connected sequence, not isolated sub-rules
body: Fitting a detention within one of the six grounds is necessary but not sufficient. Article 5(2) to (5) impose a connected sequence of procedural safeguards, each addressing a different point at which detention can become or remain arbitrary.

Article 5(2) requires prompt information, in a language the person understands, of the reasons for their arrest and any charge — without this, a person cannot meaningfully challenge their detention at all. Article 5(3) applies specifically to ground (c) detention: prompt production before a judge and trial within a reasonable time, or release pending trial. Article 5(4) gives anyone deprived of their liberty, on any ground, the right to take proceedings for a speedy court decision on the lawfulness of their continuing detention — this is the safeguard most directly engaged by the deprivation-of-liberty case law in Parts 4 and 5, because if a situation is a deprivation of liberty, someone is entitled to a periodic, genuine court review of it. Article 5(5) closes the sequence with an enforceable right to compensation where any of the above has been breached.

components.citation: European Convention on Human Rights, Article 5(4)
components.text: Everyone who is deprived of his liberty by arrest or detention shall be entitled to take proceedings by which the lawfulness of his detention shall be decided speedily by a court and his release ordered if the detention is not lawful.
elements: A deprivation of liberty (any Article 5(1) ground)
A right to take proceedings challenging its lawfulness
Release if detention is found unlawful

interaction.prompt: Put these Article 5 procedural safeguards in the order they typically apply, from the moment of detention onward.
items: Prompt information of the reasons for detention (5(2))
Prompt judicial production and trial within a reasonable time, or release pending trial (5(3))
A speedy court decision on the lawfulness of continuing detention (5(4))
An enforceable right to compensation for any breach of the above (5(5))
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence: information first, then the criminal-process-specific safeguard, then a standing right to periodic review, then compensation if any of it was breached.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Think about what a detained person needs first (to know why they're held), then what happens if they're being prosecuted, then their ongoing right to challenge continued detention, and finally what remedy follows a breach.

parts.heading: What is a 'deprivation of liberty'? Guzzardi and the old acid test
parts.voice: case-narrative, building toward a critical turn
body: Before any of the six grounds or the procedural safeguards can apply, a situation must first amount to a deprivation of liberty at all — as opposed to a lesser restriction on movement, which falls outside Article 5 entirely. Guzzardi v Italy supplies the enduring starting principle: the difference between deprivation of and restriction upon liberty is 'merely one of degree or intensity, and not one of nature or substance.' Whether someone is detained is assessed on the concrete situation they are actually in, not on how it is labelled.

For over a decade, the leading domestic gloss on that principle was the 'acid test' from P v Cheshire West and Chester Council, decided by the Supreme Court in 2014. The case concerned three individuals with learning disabilities or cognitive impairments, living under care arrangements — some in a placement, one in a supported-living setting — that involved close supervision for their own safety. The majority held that the objective element of a deprivation of liberty was satisfied wherever a person was under continuous supervision and control and was not free to leave, regardless of the person's own compliance, the normality of the setting compared to anyone else's life, or the benign purpose behind the arrangement.

Cheshire West was controversial from the moment it was decided. Its critics — including a strong dissent at the time — argued that a bright-line test focused only on supervision-and-control and freedom-to-leave, without regard to why the arrangement existed or how it compared to the ordinary lives of people with similar care needs, risked classifying enormous numbers of entirely benign caring arrangements — in care homes, supported living, and even some family settings — as 'detentions' requiring periodic court authorisation under Article 5(4), producing exactly the kind of administrative and judicial burden the doctrine was never designed to create.

components.caseName: P v Cheshire West and Chester Council
components.factsShort: Three individuals with learning disabilities or cognitive impairments lived under care arrangements involving close supervision, some restraint, and restrictions on leaving without support.
components.ratioShort: The 'acid test': a person is objectively deprived of their liberty where they are under continuous supervision and control and not free to leave, regardless of their compliance or the benign purpose of the arrangement — this specific formulation was overruled in part in 2026 (see Part 5).

expanded.facts: The three appellants each lived under care arrangements designed around their own safety and welfare needs, involving varying degrees of supervision, and in some instances physical intervention to manage behaviour that could cause harm. None had capacity to consent to the arrangements in the legal sense Article 5 requires.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The majority held that the relevant comparator for assessing whether someone is 'free to leave' is not another person with the same care needs living in a similarly restrictive arrangement, but people generally — and that the person's own apparent contentment or lack of objection to the arrangement was irrelevant to the objective question of whether they were, in fact, under continuous supervision and control and not free to leave.
expanded.significance: For over a decade, Cheshire West's acid test was the definitive statement of the objective element of deprivation of liberty in domestic law, driving a large expansion in the number of arrangements requiring formal authorisation. As Part 5 of this lesson explains, its specific formulation was overruled in part in 2026, but the case remains important as the doctrinal background against which the corrected test must be understood.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, from Guzzardi v Italy, highlight the sentence that states the general principle for distinguishing a deprivation of liberty from a mere restriction on movement — the principle that survives the 2026 overruling intact.
interaction.passage: In order to determine whether someone has been deprived of his liberty within the meaning of Article 5, the starting point must be his concrete situation, and account must be taken of a whole range of factors such as the type, duration, effects and manner of implementation of the measure in question. The difference between deprivation of and restriction upon liberty is nonetheless merely one of degree or intensity, and not one of nature or substance. This assessment cannot be reduced to a single mechanical formula, however administratively convenient that might be.
interaction.ratioSentence: The difference between deprivation of and restriction upon liberty is nonetheless merely one of degree or intensity, and not one of nature or substance.

parts.heading: 2026: the acid test overruled — the corrected law
parts.voice: doctrine-in-motion, corrective — states plainly what changed and why
body: On 2 June 2026, the Supreme Court handed down A Reference by the Attorney General for Northern Ireland [2026] UKSC 16, overruling the Cheshire West acid test in part. The Court held that reducing the deprivation-of-liberty question to a single mechanical formula — continuous supervision and control, and not free to leave — without regard to the purpose, reasonableness and relative normality of the arrangement, had drifted too far from Guzzardi's own instruction that the assessment must take account of the whole concrete situation, not a fixed checklist applied identically regardless of context.

The corrected position restores a broader, multi-factor assessment. Continuous supervision and control, and an inability to leave without permission, remain central and often decisive indicators — Cheshire West's insight that a person's own compliance or apparent contentment does not, by itself, defeat an otherwise objective finding of confinement is retained. What changes is that the purpose of the arrangement and how it compares to arrangements considered normal for a person with similar care or welfare needs are now to be weighed as part of the same objective assessment, rather than being treated as irrelevant. A restrictive but genuinely proportionate, needs-led family or supported-living arrangement is now less likely to be found a deprivation of liberty than an equivalent arrangement in an institutional setting driven by administrative convenience rather than the individual's own welfare — a distinction the acid test's bright-line formulation had no room to draw.

This is not a return to the pre-Cheshire West position the majority rejected in 2014 — the individual's own lack of objection still cannot, on its own, be treated as decisive against a finding of confinement, since that would reintroduce exactly the risk of exploited or coerced 'agreement' Cheshire West was right to guard against. It is a correction to how much weight the purpose and normality of the arrangement carry within the objective assessment, not a wholesale reversal. Get this distinction right, because 'it went back to how things were before Cheshire West' is as wrong an answer as 'nothing changed in 2026.'

components.definition: Whether a person is objectively confined — under continuous supervision and control and unable to leave without permission — assessed as part of the whole concrete situation, including the purpose of the arrangement and how it compares to arrangements normal for someone with similar care or welfare needs. The person's own compliance or lack of objection remains relevant context but is still not, on its own, decisive against a finding of confinement.

interaction.prompt: A young adult with a severe learning disability lives at home with her parents. Given her safety needs, her parents supervise her closely, accompany her whenever she leaves the house, and lock external doors overnight — arrangements a specialist social worker assesses as proportionate to her needs and materially similar to arrangements a family without her disability would adopt for a child of a similar developmental stage. Applying the corrected post-2026 test, is this arrangement more or less likely to be found a deprivation of liberty than it would have been under the pre-2026 Cheshire West acid test alone?
options: Less likely — the corrected test now weighs the proportionate, needs-led and comparatively normal character of the arrangement, factors the acid test's bright-line formulation excluded
Equally likely either way — the 2026 case made no practical difference to arrangements of this kind
More likely — the 2026 case broadened, rather than narrowed, the range of arrangements capable of being found a deprivation of liberty
interaction.explanation: Under the acid test alone, continuous supervision, control and restriction on leaving would very likely have been enough by themselves. Under the corrected test, the same objective indicators are weighed alongside the purpose and comparative normality of the arrangement — factors that, on these facts, point away from a finding of confinement, without treating her own lack of objection as decisive on its own.

testPool.prompt: Name the six permitted grounds for detention listed in Article 5(1)(a)-(f).
acceptableAnswers: conviction, non-compliance with a court order, reasonable suspicion of an offence, minors, unsound mind/addiction/vagrancy/infectious disease, immigration/deportation/extradition
testPool.modelAnswer: (a) after conviction; (b) non-compliance with a court order or to secure a legal obligation; (c) reasonable suspicion of an offence, or to prevent an offence or fleeing; (d) educational supervision of a minor; (e) persons of unsound mind, alcoholics, drug addicts, vagrants, or to prevent the spread of infectious disease; (f) to prevent unauthorised entry, or pending deportation or extradition.

testPool.prompt: Is the list of grounds in Article 5(1) exhaustive or illustrative?
options: Exhaustive — detention not falling within one of the six grounds is not permitted by Article 5
Illustrative — states may add further grounds of their own by domestic legislation

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is a genuine Article 5(1) ground for detention?
options: Detention to prevent the spread of an infectious disease
Detention because the individual holds unpopular or controversial political views
Detention purely for administrative convenience while paperwork is processed
Preventive detention of anyone assessed by the state as a general risk to public order
testPool.trapExplanation: The other three describe reasons for detention that do not correspond to any of the six recognised grounds. Only detention to prevent the spread of infectious disease, within ground (e), is genuine.

testPool.prompt: Article 5(2) requires that a person arrested be informed promptly of what, and how?
options: The reasons for the arrest and any charge, in a language they understand
Only the identity and rank of the arresting officer
Nothing beyond the bare fact that they have been arrested

testPool.prompt: Order these Article 5 procedural safeguards from the moment of detention onward.
items: Prompt information of the reasons for detention (5(2))
Prompt judicial production and trial within a reasonable time, or release pending trial (5(3))
A speedy court decision on the lawfulness of continuing detention (5(4))
An enforceable right to compensation for any breach (5(5))

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, from Guzzardi v Italy, highlight the sentence stating the general principle for identifying a deprivation of liberty.
testPool.passage: The Court's task is to examine the concrete situation of the individual concerned, taking account of a range of criteria such as the type, duration, effects and manner of implementation of the measure in question. The difference between deprivation of and restriction upon liberty is nonetheless merely one of degree or intensity, and not one of nature or substance. It follows that a person may be objectively confined even where no walls or locked doors are involved.
testPool.ratioSentence: The difference between deprivation of and restriction upon liberty is nonetheless merely one of degree or intensity, and not one of nature or substance.

testPool.prompt: Under the pre-2026 Cheshire West acid test, was a person's own apparent compliance or lack of objection to their care arrangement relevant to whether a deprivation of liberty existed?
options: No — the acid test asked only about the objective fact of continuous supervision and control and inability to leave, regardless of the person's compliance
Yes — under the acid test, a person who did not object could never be found to be deprived of their liberty

testPool.prompt: What did A Reference by the Attorney General for Northern Ireland [2026] UKSC 16 do to the Cheshire West acid test?
options: Overruled it in part, replacing its narrow supervision-and-control formulation with a broader assessment that also weighs the purpose and comparative normality of the arrangement
Confirmed the acid test as correctly stated, requiring no revision
Abolished the deprivation-of-liberty concept under Article 5 entirely
testPool.trapExplanation: The 2026 case did not abandon the objective, supervision-and-control core of the inquiry, nor did it simply confirm the old test unchanged — it corrected the acid test by requiring purpose and comparative normality to be weighed alongside it, all as part of one objective assessment.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact most relevant to whether this arrangement is a deprivation of liberty under the corrected post-2026 test.
testPool.scenarioText: A care home resident living with advanced dementia is unable to use the keypad securing the external doors and is not permitted to leave without an escort. Staff describe the arrangement as necessary purely to prevent the home from being short-staffed at exit points, rather than as a response to any specific safety assessment for this resident.
tappableSpans: unable to use the keypad securing the external doors
not permitted to leave without an escort
necessary purely to prevent the home from being short-staffed
rather than as a response to any specific safety assessment
testPool.correctSpan: rather than as a response to any specific safety assessment
testPool.explanation: The objective supervision-and-control indicators are clearly present, but the corrected test also asks why the arrangement exists. Here the stated justification is institutional convenience, not this resident's own assessed welfare needs — a factor pointing toward, not away from, a finding of confinement.

testPool.prompt: A person is detained by immigration officers while action is being taken to remove them from the country, pending completion of the necessary arrangements. Which Article 5(1) ground applies?
options: Ground (f) — detention of a person against whom action is being taken with a view to deportation
Ground (c) — reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence
Ground (e) — detention of a vagrant
testPool.explanation: This is the classic ground (f) fact pattern: detention connected to deportation or extradition proceedings, distinct from the criminal-process ground (c).

testPool.prompt: A teenager with a severe learning disability is kept under close supervision at home by his parents, who restrict unsupervised outings on the advice of his care team because of safety risks specific to his condition. Applying the corrected post-2026 test rather than the pre-2026 acid test alone, how does this affect the likelihood of a deprivation-of-liberty finding?
options: It reduces the likelihood, because the corrected test weighs the proportionate, needs-led and comparatively normal character of a family arrangement, which the acid test's bright-line formulation could not take into account
It has no effect — the corrected test applies identically to the acid test in family settings
It increases the likelihood, because the corrected test expanded the range of arrangements treated as confinement
testPool.explanation: This is exactly the kind of proportionate, needs-led family arrangement the corrected test was designed to weigh differently from an equivalent institutional arrangement driven by administrative convenience, without making the young person's own compliance decisive on its own.

testPool.prompt: Applying the corrected post-2026 test, in which scenario is a deprivation of liberty more clearly made out?
testPool.scenarioA: A resident on a locked hospital ward is under continuous staff supervision, restrained when agitated, and never permitted to leave without escort — an arrangement staff describe as driven by ward routine and staffing levels rather than any individualised care plan.
testPool.scenarioB: A resident in a supported-living flat holds a key to her own front door, comes and goes with a support worker present during the day for safety reasons specific to her own assessed needs, and is free to ask the worker to leave at any time.
testPool.explanation: Scenario A shows strong objective indicators of confinement (continuous supervision, restraint, no freedom to leave) combined with a purpose driven by institutional convenience rather than individualised need — both factors now point toward a deprivation of liberty under the corrected test. Scenario B's objective restrictions are far lighter, and its purpose is individualised and proportionate, pointing the other way.

testPool.prompt: A care home resident with a cognitive impairment is subject to continuous staff supervision and is not permitted to leave the premises unaccompanied. The home's records show the restriction was introduced following a specific, documented falls-and-wandering risk assessment for this resident, is reviewed every six weeks, and is materially similar to precautions a family might reasonably take for a relative with the same assessed risks. Applying the corrected post-2026 test, analyse whether this amounts to a deprivation of liberty.
factsToOrder: The resident is under continuous supervision and cannot leave unaccompanied
The restriction follows a specific, documented risk assessment for this resident
The arrangement is reviewed every six weeks
It is materially similar to precautions a family might reasonably take for the same assessed risks

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the resident's care arrangement amounts to a deprivation of liberty under the corrected post-2026 test.
modelAnswer.rule: Following A Reference by the Attorney General for Northern Ireland [2026] UKSC 16, a deprivation of liberty is assessed objectively by reference to continuous supervision and control and inability to leave, weighed together with the purpose of the arrangement and its comparative normality against arrangements suited to a person with similar assessed needs; the person's own compliance is not, on its own, decisive.
modelAnswer.application: The objective indicators (continuous supervision, no unaccompanied leave) are present and would very likely have satisfied the pre-2026 acid test on their own. Under the corrected test, however, the arrangement's individualised, documented basis, regular review, and comparative similarity to reasonable family precautions all weigh against a finding of confinement, distinguishing it from an equivalent restriction imposed for institutional convenience.
modelAnswer.conclusion: While finely balanced, the proportionate, needs-led and regularly reviewed character of this arrangement makes a finding of deprivation of liberty considerably less likely under the corrected post-2026 test than it would have been under the acid test alone — though the objective restriction is real enough that periodic review under Article 5(4) remains good practice regardless of the ultimate classification.

testPool.prompt: A person detained under Article 5(1)(e) is given no effective way to challenge the ongoing lawfulness of their detention for several months. Which safeguard is most directly at risk of being breached?
options: Article 5(4) — the right to a speedy court decision on the lawfulness of continuing detention
Article 5(1) itself — the detention automatically falls outside all six grounds
Article 3 — this is necessarily inhuman or degrading treatment

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is answering a deprivation-of-liberty question with the pre-2026 Cheshire West acid test alone — continuous supervision and control, not free to leave, nothing else. That test was overruled in part on 2 June 2026. The corrected test keeps those objective indicators but now weighs the purpose and comparative normality of the arrangement alongside them. Answering with 'the acid test' unqualified, after June 2026, is treated as an incomplete answer, not a correct one dressed in old language.
